name: Personal Identity
statement: What makes you the same person over time: your body, your memories, or something else?
meaning: The problem of personal identity concerns what makes a person at one time the same person, numerically identical, as a person at another time, the question of personal identity over time, also called persistence or diachronic identity. It asks for the necessary and sufficient conditions under which a person existing at one time is one and the same individual as a person existing at another time, and so what our persistence through time consists in. This is distinct from other questions sometimes labeled personal identity, such as what it is to be a person at all, or the characterization question of which traits define who one is. The main rival answers to the persistence question are three. The psychological continuity view holds that you persist in virtue of the continuity of your psychological features, memory, personality, and the like, a tradition descending from John Locke, who tied personal identity to sameness of consciousness or memory. The physical view holds that you persist in virtue of the continuity of your body or, on the animalist version associated with Eric Olson, in virtue of being the same biological organism. And the simple or further-fact view holds that personal identity is not reducible to physical or psychological continuity, perhaps consisting in an immaterial soul. Derek Parfit influentially argued that identity is not what matters in survival. The problem bears on survival, moral responsibility, self-concern, and immortality.
mechanism: The problem is posed by imagining a person at one time and a person at a later time and asking what would make them the same individual. Each answer proposes a different criterion. On the psychological continuity view, you go where your psychology goes: the later person is you if they are connected to you by an overlapping chain of psychological relations, memories, intentions, beliefs, and character. Locke launched this tradition by locating personal identity in sameness of consciousness, so that a person is the same as far as their consciousness, especially memory, extends, and he distinguished the person from the human being or underlying substance. On the physical or biological view, you go where your body or your living organism goes, so that the later person is you if they are the same body, or, for animalists, the same animal that you are, regardless of psychological change. On the simple view, there is no informative criterion at all: personal identity is a further, unanalyzable fact, perhaps the persistence of a soul. The debate is driven by thought experiments that pull these criteria apart, such as Locke's prince and the cobbler, in which a prince's consciousness enters a cobbler's body, and brain or body swaps and teletransportation, which seem to send the person with the psychology rather than the body. Derek Parfit sharpened matters with fission cases, in which each half of a divided brain is transplanted so that two later people are each psychologically continuous with the original, yet cannot both be identical to it, and concluded that identity is not what matters: what matters in survival is psychological continuity and connectedness, his Relation R, which can hold to reduced degrees or even branch.

examples.text: Locke located personal identity in sameness of consciousness, so a person is the same as far as their memory extends.
If a prince's consciousness entered a cobbler's body, Locke held the person would go with the consciousness, not the body.
If each half of your brain is transplanted, two later people are each continuous with you, so identity is not what matters.

variants.name: Psychological versus physical
variants.text: Persistence through psychological continuity, as in the Lockean tradition, versus continuity of body or organism, as in animalism.

variants.name: Identity is not what matters
variants.text: Parfit's view that what matters in survival is psychological continuity and connectedness, Relation R, not identity itself.

whyItMatters: Personal identity is one of the deepest and most gripping problems in metaphysics, because it asks what we most fundamentally are and what it takes for us to continue to exist. The question is not idle: how we answer it shapes our thinking about survival and death, about whether we could survive teleportation, brain transplants, or the uploading of our minds, and about the prospects for immortality. It bears directly on ethics and on rational self-concern, since praise, blame, punishment, promising, and prudent care for one's future self all presuppose that the future person really is oneself, and Parfit argued that reflection on fission and on the degrees of psychological continuity should transform how we regard our own future and even loosen the grip of self-interest. The Lockean shift from the persistence of a substance to the continuity of consciousness reframed the whole debate and connected personal identity to memory, mind, and moral agency. From Locke's prince and cobbler through Reid's objections to Parfit's fission cases, the problem has generated some of philosophy's most illuminating thought experiments.

working.text: ask what makes a person at one time numerically the same individual as a person at another time.
look to psychological continuity, to bodily or biological continuity, or to an unanalyzable further fact.
probe the criteria with prince-and-cobbler, teleportation, and fission cases that pull them apart.

limits: The problem of personal identity remains unresolved, and each criterion faces serious objections. Locke's memory criterion was challenged early by Thomas Reid's brave officer, or gallant officer, paradox: a general who remembers being a young officer, who in turn remembers being a flogged boy, but where the general no longer remembers being the boy, which seems to make the general both identical and not identical to the boy, violating the transitivity of identity; and by Bishop Butler's circularity objection that memory presupposes, and so cannot constitute, personal identity, since to remember doing something is already to remember oneself doing it. Refinements to psychological continuity, and rival physical and animalist views, each run into their own difficulties with the thought experiments, and animalism's claim that we are organisms is contested by cases that seem to separate person from animal. Parfit's radical conclusion that identity is not what matters is itself much debated. Some attributions and terms reward care, such as the term Relation R and the animalist Eric Olson, and Locke's discussion appears in the 1694 second edition of his Essay.
misreadings: The persistence question, what makes you the same person over time, is not the same as the characterization question of which traits define who you are; a person can change greatly in character yet remain numerically the same. Locke's criterion is about sameness of consciousness, not sameness of the underlying substance or soul, which he distinguished. And Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters is not the claim that nothing survives, but that what matters is continuity and connectedness rather than strict identity, so treating persistence as characterization, Locke's view as about substance, or Parfit as denying survival, misreads the problem.
origin: The metaphysical problem of what makes a person at one time numerically the same as a person at another, with rival psychological, physical, and simple criteria, framed by Locke's memory theory and sharpened by Parfit's fission cases.
